opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I should be careful comparing, because I only went through the ACM class myself. I never experienced the Yao Class from the inside. I've just known people from there over the years.

From my own experience, what stood out about the ACM class was that it felt very hands-on and engineering-heavy, especially early on. The culture came partly from the programming competition tradition. A lot of us had done contests, so there was a strong emphasis on actually building things, writing a lot of code, and being comfortable with systems. Implementing a compiler or other substantial projects as undergrads gave you confidence that you could make something work end to end. That turned out to matter a lot later when I moved into computer vision and deep learning. So much of research there is about getting things to actually run, debugging, and iterating quickly.

The other thing was the sense of community. The class was small, and people pushed each other. Some of that was competition, but there was also a shared feeling that you were expected to aim high, go abroad, and do serious research. Early exposure to research mattered a lot. We were encouraged to join labs and try real problems before we really knew what we were doing. That's where I first got a taste of machine learning.

My impression of the Yao Class, mostly secondhand, is that it has historically leaned more toward theory, with strong roots in theoretical computer science and mathematical rigor. That produces a different kind of strength: people who think very cleanly about problems from first principles. I wouldn't say one is better. They're different flavors. Both programs are really about taking talented students, putting them together, and giving them unusually early access to research and to a global perspective. In the end, the people you're surrounded by probably shape you as much as the curriculum does.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I can really only speak from the inside about ACM class, because that's where I was — I was in the SJTU ACM class, Yu Yong's program. Yao Class I know mostly from friends and from the people who came out of it, so take that half with a grain of salt.

The thing that stands out to me about ACM class is how early and how hard it pushed you toward research. It wasn't framed as "you're an undergraduate, learn the fundamentals, and maybe later you'll do research." From the first or second year, the expectation was that you'd be in a lab, reading papers, trying things. A lot of us were sent out to places like Microsoft Research Asia as interns, and that was a huge deal for me. I think I got my first real taste of what research actually feels like — the frustration of it, not just the romantic version — at MSRA while still an undergrad. That shaped the whole trajectory afterward.

The other thing was the competitive programming culture, obviously — it's in the name. There's a kind of brutal, honest feedback loop in ACM-ICPC. Your code either passes or it doesn't. Nobody cares about your explanation. I think that trains a certain engineering toughness and a willingness to just sit and debug for hours, and honestly that has carried over into deep learning research more than people might expect. A lot of what we do day to day is debugging.

Yao Class, from what I can see, was built a bit more around the theory side. Andrew Yao's background is theoretical computer science, so the curriculum had this very strong mathematical core — algorithms, complexity, that kind of thing. The people I know from Yao Class tend to have a very clean, rigorous way of thinking about problems. When they come into machine learning, they often bring a kind of formal clarity that I think the rest of us had to pick up later.

So if I had to simplify: ACM class was "throw you in the water early and let you learn to swim in a real lab," and Yao Class was "give you a very deep foundation first." Both approaches clearly produced a lot of people who ended up doing well. I'd say I benefited from the ACM style because I was impatient — I wanted to touch real problems — but I've also spent years trying to backfill some of the mathematical maturity that Yao Class students seemed to have from the start.

And actually, one thing I'd add is that both programs did something that I think is underrated, which is that they put a small group of very motivated people together and let them push each other. The curriculum matters, but the peers mattered more. I still work with people from that era, and some of my sense of what "good" looks like really came from watching classmates.

r001.rationale: The response describes ACM’s competitive programming culture as intense, but does not suggest it was less competitive than Yao Class.

astra-6.text: I can speak more directly about SJTU’s ACM class; I don’t have the same firsthand perspective on the Yao Class. What stands out to me is the emphasis on building a strong foundation and learning to solve difficult problems independently. Programming and algorithms give you very concrete feedback: you might think you understand something, but implementing it exposes the gaps. And being surrounded by classmates who approach the same problem differently pushes you to question your own thinking. I’d be cautious about making a sharp comparison between the two programs, but those are the aspects of the ACM training I would emphasize.

sol-6.1.text: I can’t make a firsthand comparison with the Yao Class, but what stood out to me about SJTU’s ACM class was the intensity of learning alongside very strong peers. You weren’t just absorbing material from lectures; you were constantly being challenged by how other students approached a problem. There was a strong emphasis on mathematical foundations, algorithms, and actually working through difficult problems. I’d be cautious about saying one program is better—the part I can speak to is how much that environment pushed me to become an independent learner.
